guidance: Take the mesh count, thread diameter and fabric caliper from the same fabric data sheet, because a count without its thread diameter says little: at one count a thinner thread leaves a wider opening and passes more ink. Check the reported per-inch and per-centimetre figures against the sheet. The open area and ink volume describe a flat, new, tensioned fabric; the stencil, the ink, the squeegee and the substrate all change what reaches the print, so use the figure to compare meshes and to order ink, then confirm the deposit with a test print.
method: The mesh count is converted to threads per inch when it is given per centimetre (multiply by 2.54). The pitch is 25400 divided by the count in threads per inch, in micrometres, because an inch is 25400 micrometres; the mesh opening is the pitch minus the thread diameter; the open area is the opening divided by the pitch, squared, as a percentage; and the theoretical ink volume is that open fraction multiplied by the fabric thickness, reported in cubic centimetres per square metre. One micrometre of film over one square metre is one cubic centimetre, so the same number is the theoretical wet film thickness in micrometres. The print area is the width times the height, converted from inches to millimetres when needed, and the ink per print is the volume per square metre times the area in square metres in millilitres; grams use the ink density, and the run total multiplies by the number of prints. Counts are accepted from 10 to 500 threads per inch, or 4 to 200 threads per centimetre; thread diameters from 10 to 400 micrometres; fabric thicknesses from 20 to 1000 micrometres; print sides from 1 to 2000 millimetres (0.04 to 78.74 inches); the number of prints from 1 to 100000 as a whole number; and ink densities from 0.8 to 2.0 grams per millilitre. A thread diameter that leaves less than one micrometre of opening is refused, because the fabric is physically impossible at that count. Warnings appear below 20% open area (a fine mesh that heavy-body, metallic and glitter inks cannot pass), above 60% open area (a coarse mesh that holds little fine detail) and above a litre for the run. The page does not model the stencil thickness, the ink film lost to the squeegee, shear thinning, penetration into the substrate, mesh crimp, calendering, twill weave, or the difference between nominal and measured apertures, so its figure is a geometric ceiling for comparison rather than a prediction of the printed deposit.

sources.title: SaatiPrint, Tech Tips for Screen Printers: the theoretical ink deposit Vth = (w / (w + d)) squared times D in cm3 per m2, with w the mesh aperture, d the wire diameter and D the cloth thickness, and the note that the figure is theoretical and meant for comparing fabrics.

Screen Printing Magazine, How Much Ink Do You Need?: estimating the wet ink deposit from mesh count, thread diameter and fabric thickness, then multiplying by the image area and the length of the run.

Polyester, nylon and stainless steel screen printing mesh catalogue: published apertures, open areas, calipers and theoretical ink volumes for real fabrics, for example 250 mesh with a 40 micrometre thread giving a 62 micrometre aperture, 36.8% open area and 34 cm3 per m2.
